tagline: The last of the prophets argues with a tired, disillusioned people and promises that the Lord will send his messenger and come to his temple.
overview:
Malachi is the final book of the Old Testament in Christian Bibles and the last of the twelve shorter prophets. It speaks to Jews in Judah a few generations after the return from exile. The temple has been rebuilt and the sacrifices restored, but the great future the earlier prophets promised has not arrived. The people are still poor, still ruled by Persia, and increasingly cynical. Priests offer blind and lame animals, men divorce the wives of their youth, tithes go unpaid, and ordinary believers ask whether serving God is worth it at all.

The book is built as a series of arguments. God makes a statement, the people push back with a question (How have you loved us? How have we despised your name?), and God answers with evidence. Through these exchanges Malachi exposes a faith that has gone through the motions while its heart went cold, and he calls priests and people back to covenant loyalty. Then he looks forward: God will send his messenger to prepare the way, the Lord will suddenly come to his temple to refine his people like silver, and before the great day of the LORD Elijah the prophet will come to turn the hearts of fathers and children.

That promise matters enormously for the Bible as a whole. The Old Testament in its Christian order closes on the expectation of a coming messenger and an Elijah, and the New Testament opens with John the Baptist, dressed like Elijah, preparing the way for Jesus. Malachi is the hinge between the two.
author: The book's heading attributes it to Malachi (1:1), and nothing else is known of him. The name means my messenger, the same Hebrew form used in 3:1 (My messenger), which has led some to ask whether it is a title rather than a personal name. The ancient Greek translation, the Septuagint, rendered 1:1 as by the hand of his messenger, and some early Jewish tradition identified the author with Ezra. The heading also resembles those at Zechariah 9:1 and 12:1, and many critical scholars suggest the book was originally an anonymous oracle given a name drawn from 3:1. Many other scholars, conservative and critical alike, take Malachi as a real prophet's name, noting that every other prophetic book is attributed to a named person and that similar names are attested. Either way, the book presents itself as the word of the LORD through a messenger, and its authority has never rested on knowing more about him.
date: The book gives no date, but its details point clearly to the Persian period after the exile. The temple is standing and sacrifices are offered (1:7-10), so it comes after 515 BC. Judah is under a governor, the Persian-era title used in 1:8. The abuses Malachi attacks, corrupt priests, marriages to women who worship other gods, and neglected tithes, are the same ones Ezra and Nehemiah confronted (Ezra 9-10; Nehemiah 13). Most scholars therefore date Malachi to the middle of the fifth century BC, around 470 to 430 BC. Some place it shortly before Ezra's arrival in 458 BC or Nehemiah's first term as governor beginning in 445 BC, preparing the ground for their reforms; others place it during the interval around Nehemiah's second visit, when the same problems had returned.
setting:
Judah was a small province, called Yehud, within the vast Persian Empire, ruled from Susa and Persepolis under kings such as Artaxerxes I (who reigned from 465 to 424 BC). Jerusalem was a modest town, and for much of this period its walls lay in ruins until Nehemiah rebuilt them. The returned exiles had been promised glory by Haggai and Zechariah, who urged the temple's rebuilding around 520 to 515 BC, but decades later there was no Davidic king, no wealth of the nations flowing in, and no visible sign that God was keeping his word.

That long disappointment bred a quiet cynicism. Priests treated the altar as a chore, offering sick animals they would never dare present to the governor. Men married women from surrounding peoples and discarded their first wives. Farmers held back the tithe that supported the Levites. And the devout watched the arrogant prosper and wondered aloud what they had gained by fearing the LORD. Meanwhile Edom, Judah's old rival to the southeast, had been devastated, its land slowly taken over by Arab peoples, and Malachi points to that ruin as evidence that God still distinguishes between nations.
purpose: Malachi was written to call a discouraged and compromised community back to wholehearted covenant faithfulness. It confronts the priests first, because they had corrupted worship and instruction, and then the people, for unfaithfulness in marriage, in giving, and in speech about God. Its deeper purpose is to answer the question behind all the complaints: does God still love us, and does faithfulness matter? Malachi answers yes on both counts, grounds that answer in God's unchanging character (3:6), and gives the faithful a future to wait for: a coming messenger, a coming Lord, a day that will burn like a furnace for the arrogant and rise like the sun for those who fear his name.
story: Malachi comes at the end of the Old Testament's story of return. After the Babylonian exile, Cyrus of Persia allowed the Jews to go home in 539/538 BC; the temple was rebuilt under Zerubbabel with the urging of Haggai and Zechariah; and Ezra and Nehemiah later reformed the community and rebuilt Jerusalem's walls. Malachi speaks into that same world, a generation or two after the temple's completion, when the energy of return has faded. In Christian Bibles, which follow the order of the Greek Old Testament, it is the last book before the Gospels, so its closing promise of Elijah leads straight into the New Testament. In the Hebrew Bible, Malachi closes the section of the Prophets, and the Writings follow, ending with Chronicles. Around four centuries pass between Malachi and the birth of Jesus, years of Persian, Greek, and then Roman rule.
christ:
The Gospels open where Malachi ends. Malachi 3:1 promises a messenger who will prepare the way before the LORD, and Mark begins his Gospel by quoting it together with Isaiah 40:3 (Mark 1:2-3). Jesus himself identifies John the Baptist as the messenger of Malachi 3:1 (Matthew 11:10) and says that John is the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14; 17:10-13). The angel's announcement of John's birth uses Malachi 4:6, saying John will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children (Luke 1:17). John himself, asked whether he was Elijah, said he was not (John 1:21), which most interpreters take to mean he was not Elijah returned in person, while he did come in the spirit and power of Elijah.

If John is the messenger who prepares the way, then the one who comes after him is the Lord who comes to his temple (3:1). The New Testament makes that identification of Jesus with the LORD of Israel quietly but unmistakably. Malachi's refining fire, his promise of pure offerings among the nations (1:11), and his sun of righteousness rising with healing (4:2) have all been read by Christians in light of Christ's coming, though these readings are more thematic than direct quotations.
reading: Read Malachi as a set of disputations: listen for the pattern of God's claim, the people's objection, and God's reply, and notice how the objections expose the people's hearts. The book is prophecy in prose with poetic touches, not a law code, so its sharp statements (Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated; I hate divorce) should be read within the argument each is making rather than lifted out as freestanding rules. Be aware that Hebrew Bibles have only three chapters; English 4:1-6 is Hebrew 3:19-24. Two common misreadings are worth avoiding. The tithing passage (3:6-12) is sometimes turned into a promise of personal wealth, but it addresses a covenant community's support of temple worship and its trust in God's provision. And the book's hard words against the priests and people are not the whole message; they sit inside God's opening declaration, I have loved you.

structure.title: God's love for Jacob
structure.summary: The first disputation answers the question how God has loved Israel by pointing to his choice of Jacob over Esau and the ruin of Edom.

structure.title: The priests who despise God's name
structure.summary: God indicts the priests for offering defective animals and for corrupting their calling to teach, contrasting them with the covenant faithfulness of Levi.

structure.title: Faithlessness in marriage
structure.summary: The people break faith with God and with one another by marrying worshipers of foreign gods and divorcing the wives of their youth.

structure.title: The coming messenger and the Lord's refining
structure.summary: To those who ask where the God of justice is, the LORD promises a messenger to prepare his way and his own sudden coming to refine and judge.

structure.title: Return and bring the tithe
structure.summary: God calls the people to return to him and to stop robbing him in tithes and offerings, promising blessing if they trust him.

structure.title: The day that is coming
structure.summary: To those who say serving God is futile, God promises a scroll of remembrance, a day of burning for the arrogant and healing for the faithful, and Elijah before the great day of the LORD.

themes.title: God's steadfast love
themes.body: The book begins with God's declaration, I have loved you, and every rebuke that follows is spoken from within that love. The choice of Jacob, the covenant with Levi, the covenant of marriage, and the unchanging character of the LORD (3:6) all rest on a love that precedes Israel's response and outlasts its failures.

themes.title: Worship that honors God
themes.body: Malachi insists that how people worship reveals what they think of God. Blind and lame sacrifices, grudging tithes, and bored priests say that God is not worth the best. The book contrasts that contempt with a coming day when God's name will be great among the nations and pure offerings will be brought in every place.

themes.title: Covenant faithfulness
themes.body: Covenant is the book's backbone: the covenant with Levi (2:4-8), the covenant of the fathers (2:10), the covenant of marriage (2:14), and the messenger of the covenant (3:1). Unfaithfulness to God and unfaithfulness to one another are treated as the same sin seen from two sides.

themes.title: The coming day of the LORD
themes.body: Against the complaint that God does not act, Malachi promises that he will: a messenger will prepare the way, the Lord will come to his temple, and a day is coming that will distinguish the righteous from the wicked. That day brings refining fire and burning for the arrogant, and healing and joy for those who fear God's name.

themes.title: Honest questions and cynical ones
themes.body: The people's questions run through the book, and Malachi distinguishes between them. Some are defensive evasions (How have we despised your name?). Some are the cynicism of people who have decided God does not care. And some come from the faithful who fear the LORD and talk together in their perplexity, and God listens and writes their names in a book of remembrance (3:16).

keyChapters.why: God's declaration of love and his rebuke of worthless worship set the terms of the whole book, and 1:11 promises that God's name will be great among the nations.
The chapter joins the corruption of the priesthood with unfaithfulness in marriage and gives one of the Old Testament's strongest statements of marriage as a covenant witnessed by God.
The promise of the messenger who prepares the way and the Lord who comes to his temple is quoted in the Gospels and applied to John the Baptist and Jesus.
The Old Testament's final words point back to the law of Moses and forward to Elijah, and the New Testament opens by answering them.

parts.body:
Malachi is the last of the twelve shorter prophets and, in Christian Bibles, the last book of the Old Testament. It speaks to Judah a few generations after the return from exile. The temple has been rebuilt and the sacrifices restored, but the great future the earlier prophets promised has not come. The people are still poor and still ruled by Persia, and a quiet cynicism has set in.

The book opens with God's love: ‘I have loved you,’ says the LORD (1:2). Then it argues. God makes a claim, the people push back with a question, and God answers with evidence. Priests offer blind and lame animals. Men divorce the wives of their youth. Tithes go unpaid. And faithful people ask whether serving God is worth it at all.

Then the book looks ahead. God will send his messenger to prepare the way, and the Lord will suddenly come to his temple as a refiner's fire (3:1-2). Before the great day of the LORD, Elijah the prophet will come to turn the hearts of fathers and children to one another (4:5-6). The New Testament opens with John the Baptist, preparing the way for Jesus.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
The exiles began coming home after Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC. Urged on by Haggai and Zechariah, they finished the temple in 515 BC. Judah was a small province of the Persian Empire, ruled by a governor, under kings such as Artaxerxes the First, who reigned from 465 to 424 BC. For much of this time Jerusalem's walls lay in ruins, until Nehemiah rebuilt them.

Decades after the temple was finished there was still no king from David's line, no wealth of the nations flowing in, and no visible sign that God was keeping his word. That long disappointment bred the cynicism Malachi confronts. Edom, Judah's old rival to the southeast, had meanwhile been laid waste, and Malachi points to its ruin as a sign that God still keeps faith with Jacob.

The heading gives the book to Malachi (1:1), and nothing else is known of him. The name is the Hebrew word for messenger with a possessive ending, the form God uses in 3:1 for the messenger he will send, which has led some to ask whether it is a title rather than a name. The ancient Greek translation read 1:1 as by the hand of his messenger, and some early Jewish tradition named Ezra as the author. Many critical scholars suggest the book was first an unnamed oracle given a name drawn from 3:1, since its heading resembles those at Zechariah 9:1 and 12:1. Many other scholars, conservative and critical alike, take Malachi as a real prophet's name, noting that every other prophetic book is credited to a named person.

The book gives no date, but its details point to the Persian period. The temple is standing and sacrifices are offered, so it comes after 515 BC. Judah has a governor (1:8). And the abuses Malachi attacks, careless priests, marriages to women who worship other gods, and unpaid tithes, are the ones Ezra and Nehemiah confronted. Most scholars date the book to the middle of the fifth century BC, about 470 to 430 BC. Some place it shortly before Ezra came in 458 BC or Nehemiah in 445 BC; others place it around Nehemiah's second visit, when the same problems had returned.

Malachi is a series of six arguments, often called disputations. Each follows the same pattern. God makes a statement. The people object with a question, introduced by but you ask. God answers with evidence. Listen for the objections, because they show what the people really think of God: ‘How have You loved us?’ (1:2), ‘How have we despised Your name?’ (1:6), ‘How have we wearied Him?’ (2:17), ‘How can we return?’ (3:7).

The six run from God's love for Jacob (1:1-5), to the priests (1:6 to 2:9), to marriage (2:10-16), to the coming messenger (2:17 to 3:5), to the tithe (3:6-12), and to the day that is coming (3:13 to 4:3). The book closes with two words: remember the law of Moses, and watch for Elijah (4:4-6).

Hebrew Bibles have only three chapters. The English 4:1-6 is Hebrew 3:19-24.

The book's first word from God is love. ‘I have loved you,’ says the LORD. But you ask, ‘How have You loved us?’ (1:2). God answers by pointing to Jacob and Esau, the twin brothers whose families became Israel and Edom. ‘Yet Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated’ (1:2-3), and Edom's land lies in ruins while Israel has been brought home.

In Hebrew, love and hate set side by side often mean choosing and not choosing. Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and Genesis says Leah was unloved. Genesis also shows God giving Esau land and descendants. The line speaks first of two nations and God's choice of Jacob's line to carry his covenant.

Paul quotes it in Romans 9:13 to argue that God's promises never rested on descent or effort but on his free choosing. How far that argument reaches is debated, and this site takes no side. Reformed interpreters read Romans 9 as teaching God's choice of individuals for salvation. Many Arminian and other interpreters read it as God's choice of peoples and roles in the story of redemption, noting that Malachi speaks of nations. Both agree that God's choosing is grace, never earned.

The priests despise God's name, and they cannot see it. They offer blind, lame and sick animals, which the law forbade. “Try offering them to your governor! Would he be pleased with you or show you favor?” (1:8). God would rather someone shut the temple doors than let the useless fires go on. They call the altar a nuisance and turn up their noses at it.

Against that, God sets two pictures. His name will be great among the nations, ‘from where the sun rises to where it sets’ (1:11). And he recalls what a priest was meant to be. Of Levi, ‘True instruction was in his mouth, and nothing false was found on his lips’ (2:6). ‘For the lips of a priest should preserve knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth’ (2:7). Priests who show partiality in teaching God's law cause many to stumble, and God holds them to account.

‘Do we not all have one Father? Did not one God create us?’ (2:10). The people have broken faith with God and with one another. Men of Judah married women who worshiped other gods, and some divorced the wives they married when young. In a small, poor province, a new marriage could bring land and standing; for the wife sent away it could mean poverty and disgrace. God says he has been a witness between a man and ‘the wife of your youth’, his ‘companion’ and his ‘wife by covenant’ (2:14).

The Hebrew of 2:16 is among the hardest in the prophets, and translations differ. The BSB reads, ‘For I hate divorce,’ says the LORD, the God of Israel. Several recent translations take the man as the subject instead, so that the verse condemns the man who hates and divorces his wife. On either reading the verse condemns a man who discards a faithful wife, and it calls that act violence. The passage is aimed at men who were breaking covenant, not at those who were abandoned or wronged. Scripture allows divorce in some cases, and Christians differ on which. This passage never asks anyone to stay where they are being harmed.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

parts.h: The messenger, the refiner, and the tithe
parts.body:
The people have wearied God by asking, ‘Where is the God of justice?’ (2:17). He answers that he is coming. ‘Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me. Then the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple’ (3:1). But that coming is not comfortable. ‘For He will be like a refiner’s fire, like a launderer’s soap’ (3:2). He will purify the priests first, then judge those who cheat workers of their wages and oppress the widow, the fatherless and the foreigner (3:5).

‘Because I, the LORD, do not change, you descendants of Jacob have not been destroyed’ (3:6). Then the call: ‘Return to Me, and I will return to you’ (3:7). The people are robbing God by holding back the tithe, the tenth that fed the Levites and the poor through the temple storehouse. God tells them to bring the full tithe and test him, and he will open the windows of heaven (3:10).

Verse 10 is sometimes used to promise wealth to anyone who tithes. The good it names is rain and harvest for a farming people under the covenant of Moses, in a time of scarcity. Christians differ on whether the tenth remains the standard for believers or whether the New Testament's call to generous, cheerful giving replaces a fixed share. Neither reading makes giving a technique for getting rich.

parts.h: The scroll of remembrance, and Elijah
parts.body:
Some say, ‘It is futile to serve God’ (3:14). The arrogant prosper and evildoers escape. Then the book does something rare in the prophets: it stops quoting God and tells what people did. ‘At that time those who feared the LORD spoke with one another, and the LORD listened and heard them’ (3:16). A scroll of remembrance is written, and God calls them his treasured possession.

The coming day will burn like a furnace for the arrogant. ‘But for you who fear My name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings’ (4:2), and they will leap like calves let out of the stall.

The book ends looking back and looking forward. ‘Remember the law of My servant Moses’ (4:4). ‘Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD’ (4:5). He will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and of children to their fathers (4:6). In synagogue reading it became the custom to repeat verse 5 after verse 6, so that the prophets would not end on the word curse.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Malachi
parts.body:
The Gospels open where Malachi ends. Mark begins with Malachi 3:1 joined to Isaiah 40:3, under Isaiah's name: ‘Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way’ (Mark 1:2). Jesus said of John the Baptist, ‘This is the one about whom it is written’ (Matthew 11:10), and quoted 3:1. He said of John, ‘he is the Elijah who was to come’ (Matthew 11:14), and the angel who announced John's birth said he would go ‘in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to their children’ (Luke 1:17).

Yet when John was asked, ‘Are you Elijah?’ he said, ‘I am not’ (John 1:21). Most interpreters take this to mean he was not Elijah returned in person but came in Elijah's spirit and power. Christians differ on whether the promise has a further fulfillment before Christ's return; this site takes no side.

Paul quotes 1:2-3 in Romans 9:13. These are the New Testament's own lines from Malachi, and these notes draw no others.

Read the book as a set of arguments, and listen to the people's questions; readers still ask them.

Read the hard lines inside the argument each is making, not as freestanding rules: the lines about Jacob and Esau, about divorce, and about the tithe. And remember where the book begins. Every rebuke sits inside God's first word, that he has loved them.

Read the ending slowly. The last prophet of the Old Testament points back to Moses and forward to Elijah, and the next voice in a Christian Bible is a man dressed like Elijah, preaching by the Jordan.

hard.line: Jacob loved and Esau hated, and Paul's use of the line in Romans 9.
Blind and lame offerings: worship that gives God the leftovers.
Dung on the priests' faces: a deliberately shocking threat.
Marrying the daughter of a foreign god: worship, not ethnicity.
Hating divorce: a hard verse, and what it means for those divorced or in danger.
Who is the messenger, and who is the Lord who comes to his temple?
Testing God with the tithe: does tithing promise wealth?
Was John the Baptist Elijah, and is Elijah still to come?

words.line: Massa, a prophet's heavy word, the heading of the book (1:1).
The prophet's name, the same Hebrew word God uses in 3:1 for the messenger he will send (1:1).
An argument: God's claim, the people's question, God's answer, six times over.
Words that, set side by side, often mean choosing and not choosing (1:2-3).
The altar, pictured as the place where God receives his people's gifts (1:7, 12).
Berit, the bond with Levi, between the fathers, and between husband and wife (2:4-14).
A first wife married when both were young (2:14-15).
The one sent to prepare the way before the LORD (3:1).
The furnace that melts silver until it is pure (3:2-3).
A tenth of the harvest, for the Levites and the poor through the temple storehouse (3:8-10).
The record written before God of those who feared him (3:16).
Segullah, a king's own treasure, the word God used of Israel at Sinai (3:17).
The dawn that rises with healing on those who fear God's name (4:2).
The prophet promised before the great day of the LORD (4:5).
